subcategory: pond margin and rain garden rush

planting.note: Divide clumps in late winter or early spring and plant into moist to seasonally wet soil in full sun for the tightest, most upright blue-gray form; divide congested clumps every 3-4 years.

directions: Only a named cultivar of this species was previously represented in this dataset — the plain wild species itself is a blue-gray evergreen clumping rush that holds its color year-round and tolerates both coastal fog and real summer drought once established. Plant it in moist to seasonally wet soil in full sun; in shade or on the hot side of its range it tends to flop and lose color saturation. It makes one of the few rushes genuinely suited to Mediterranean-climate gardens without dedicated irrigation infrastructure.

planting.note: Divide rhizome clumps in spring and plant at a pond or stream margin; contain within small ornamental ponds, since it spreads steadily by rhizome.

directions: Unlike most rushes grown for stiff vertical stems, this species is grown for its broad, iris-like flat foliage and bronze-copper flower clusters from midsummer into fall. Pair it at pond margins where its broader leaf texture contrasts with round-stemmed rushes and bulrushes. It spreads steadily by rhizome, making it useful for streambank stabilization, but it should be contained in a small ornamental pond rather than left to colonize freely.

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring and plant into consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in a constructed bog garden or the shaded margin of a woodland pond.

directions: A cold-hardy northern rush of boreal bogs, fens, and beaver-pond shorelines, this species fills a niche none of the more southern or western rushes already in cultivation cover. It needs consistently moist to wet, acidic soil, matching a constructed bog garden or the shaded margin of a woodland pond in cold climates where the common weedy rushes are overused defaults. It tolerates full sun to light shade along naturalistic wet edges.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes or sow seed in spring into full sun and consistently moist to wet soil at a pond edge or wet prairie swale; give it room, since it spreads moderately by rhizome.

directions: Large, showy, ball-like flower clusters make this one of the more architectural rushes available, with a bolder textural draw than foliage-only species. Give it full sun and consistently moist to wet soil at a pond edge or wet prairie swale, where its globular, spiky flower heads provide strong seasonal texture. It spreads moderately by rhizome, so give it room or confine it with a barrier in a small bed.

planting.note: Broadcast seed onto bare, exposed wet mud at a pond edge or freshly excavated rain garden basin in full sun to light shade; self-sows readily once established.

directions: A fine-textured, diffusely branched southeastern wetland rush, this species carries a loose, airy habit distinct from the stiffer, tighter-clumping rushes already common in cultivation. It favors disturbed, bare wet mud and ditches, making it useful for naturalizing a freshly excavated rain garden basin or pond edge where a loose flower and seed-head texture is wanted among emergent pond plants. It self-sows readily where soil stays wet.

planting.note: Divide small colonies in spring and plant into full sun to part sun at a pond edge or wet prairie planting; tolerates drier soil better than most bulrushes once established.

directions: Closely resembling the already common woolgrass but with brighter yellow-green foliage and distinctly drooping, rust-colored seed heads, this bulrush gives a softer silhouette than the stiffer, upright species. It tolerates drier soils better than most Scirpus, bridging the gap between true emergent wetland plantings and average moist perennial borders. Mass it at a pond edge or in a wet prairie planting for the best display of its nodding seed heads.

planting.note: Divide rhizome clumps in spring and plant at the shaded edge of a woodland pond; stout rhizomes form broad colonies, so site it in a naturalized rather than tightly bordered feature.

directions: One of the few bulrushes that genuinely performs in partial shade, this large, robust species is useful at the shaded edge of a woodland pond where sun-loving bulrushes and other emergent sedges struggle. Its stout, creeping rhizomes form broad colonies over time, suiting naturalized plantings better than tight formal pond baskets. It also carries ethnobotanical history as a basket-fiber and food plant for Pacific Northwest Indigenous communities.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring and plant in a large pond, retention basin, or naturalized shoreline with a root barrier if space is limited; this species spreads assertively.

directions: A large, structural, freshwater bulrush distinct from the brackish-coast Bolboschoenus already in cultivation, this species is best suited to big water features, retention basins, or naturalized shorelines rather than small ornamental ponds. Its triangular stems and large seed heads give strong winter structure and valuable waterfowl forage. Confine it with a root barrier in any space-limited planting, since it spreads aggressively by rhizome once established.

planting.note: Divide the slow-spreading rhizome and plant directly into a submerged aquatic basket in permanent shallow water rather than merely moist soil.

directions: This spikerush carries sharply four-angled, spongy stems rather than the round stems of other spikerushes already in cultivation, giving it a distinctly sculptural, geometric quality at a pond margin. It is an obligate wetland plant that needs permanent shallow water, so plant it directly into a submerged aquatic basket rather than a border bed. Use it where a stronger architectural accent is wanted among softer round-stemmed companions.

planting.note: Broadcast seed onto exposed, sunny, saturated mud in a freshly dug rain garden basin or drawn-down pond margin; self-sows reliably where soil stays wet.

directions: Unlike the perennial spikerushes already in cultivation, this is a true annual that germinates on exposed wet mud and completes its life cycle within a single growing season. That makes it valuable as a fast pioneer or nurse plant for quickly covering bare soil on a freshly dug rain garden basin or newly drawn-down pond margin while slower perennials establish. It needs full sun and saturated soil to perform, and reseeds reliably wherever those conditions persist.

planting.note: Root culm-tip plantlets or divide clumps in spring and plant into alkaline, mineral-rich wet soil such as a calcareous bog feature or spring-fed water garden; source only nursery-propagated material, never wild-collected stock, since it is rare or protected in several states.

directions: This spikerush has a signature 'walking' habit found nowhere else on this list — its arching stems bend down and root at the tip, slowly colonizing bare wet ground as they go. It specifically needs genuinely alkaline, mineral-rich wet soil such as a fen or marl flat and will struggle in ordinary acidic rain-garden soil, making it a specialist choice for a calcareous bog feature or spring-fed water garden rather than a general-purpose pond plant. Because it is listed as rare or threatened in several states, source only nursery-propagated culm-tip cuttings or divisions.
